problem: Most VLN methods since Speaker-Follower use a high-level action space in which the agent teleports between navigable viewpoints on a nav graph. This depends on simulator prior knowledge and removes the embodied nature of the task. Low-level action VLN models lag far behind in performance.
motivation: An embodied agent should output the low-level movements it can actually perform, without being told navigable directions. Instructions are long and change what the agent must attend to over time, so the visual features should be conditioned on the part of the instruction being executed. Comparing low-level and high-level models directly is unfair, so the field needs a taxonomy.
key_idea: Generate 1x1 dynamic convolutional filters from the currently attended instruction segment, apply them to the panoramic visual feature grid, and feed the response maps to an LSTM policy that predicts low-level actions (turn, elevate, forward, stop).
insight: Ablations show that dynamic filters beat fixed convolution (val-unseen SR 31.6 vs 21.8 for the seq2seq baseline), that instruction attention helps (22.0 to 31.6 SR val-unseen), and that GloVe embeddings help (25.8 to 31.6). Four filters is best; more filters degrade performance. Once models are separated by action space, results within each group are far more consistent.
method: Instruction encoder: stop words removed, GloVe embeddings, LSTM (hidden 512) producing per-word states X

Visual encoder: 360° panorama discretized into a 12x3 grid (30° steps, 3 elevations), ResNet-152 ImageNet features (2048-d) reduced to 512 with a bottleneck, plus (sin φ, cos φ, sin θ) coordinates relative to the agent's heading and elevation
Encoder-decoder attention: query from previous policy hidden state, scaled dot-product attention over the instruction states, giving the current instruction piece s_t
Dynamic convolution: f_t = L2norm(tanh(W s_t + b)) yields 4 1x1 filters, convolved with the visual features (equivalent to dot-product attention), scaled by sqrt(d_f)

Policy: an LSTM on the flattened response maps and the previous action outputs a softmax over 6 actions (left 30°, right 30°, up, down, forward, end); trained with cross-entropy against simulator ground-truth actions, sampling during training and argmax at test
Data augmentation: extra synthetic instructions from Speaker-Follower for the final model

setting.backbone: ResNet-152 (frozen features) + GloVe + LSTM encoder/policy with dynamic filters (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: R2R train set; final variant adds Speaker-Follower synthetic augmented instructions
setting.observation: panoramic 360° RGB discretized into a 12x3 grid of ResNet-152 features
setting.action_space: low-level: turn left 30°, turn right 30°, raise elevation, lower elevation, go ahead, end episode
setting.privileged: none at test time (ground-truth low-level actions from the nav graph are used for supervision in training only)

results: With Speaker-Follower augmentation, the dynamic-filter model reaches 35% SR / 0.31 SPL on R2R test-unseen. This is the best low-level-action result, beating the Student-forcing baseline (20% SR) and RPA (25% SR). It is also competitive with some high-level models: SPL is above Speaker-Follower (0.28) and near Self-Monitoring (0.32), but below Regretful (48% SR).
limitations: Still clearly behind high-level-action methods such as Regretful (48% SR) and Self-Monitoring (43% SR) on test-unseen, with a large seen/unseen gap
Training uses ground-truth low-level actions derived from the nav graph, and the evaluation covers only R2R in simulation with no real robot
Fixed panorama discretization and frozen ImageNet features; filter count must be tuned
